title: Moderated or Unmoderated: Choose by Learning Risk
editorial_note: Automated dialogue draft from the revised lesson. Review spoken wording and meaning before publishing.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Today we're talking about Moderated or Unmoderated: Choose by Learning Risk. By the end, you'll know why this matters, how to use it, and what to notice in a real product.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What is the problem we are trying to understand?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: In moderated evaluation, a researcher introduces the study, observes in real time, probes interpretation, adapts follow-up, manages technology, and responds to distress or unexpected situations. This is valuable when mental models, ambiguity, emotion, accessibility, complex context, or novel system behaviour matter.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at what moderation changes?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Moderation also changes behaviour. Participants may seek approval, explain more than they would naturally, avoid criticism, or succeed because the moderator rescues them. Skilled moderation uses neutral prompts and a consistent assistance ladder, and reports interventions.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: In unmoderated evaluation, participants complete tasks independently, usually remotely and asynchronously. Instructions and instrumentation must carry the study. It offers scheduling flexibility, geographic reach, consistent task presentation, and larger structured samples at lower marginal cost.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: It is useful for stable flows with clear success criteria, comparative benchmarks, first-click or navigation studies, and directional performance patterns.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: But researchers cannot clarify ambiguity, confirm environment reliably, probe unexpected behaviour, or protect participants immediately. A larger sample does not repair a poorly specified task or an unobservable mental model.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at use a mode decision matrix?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Assess:

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: need to understand reasoning rather than only behaviour; task and prototype stability; ambiguity of instructions and success criteria; sensitivity, distress, or safety risk; need for adaptive probing; accessibility support and technology complexity; importance of natural environment; need for breadth, comparison, or statistical precision; ability to verify participants and data quality; consequence of misinterpreting the result.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Choose a hybrid when questions differ. Moderated exploration can develop valid tasks and explanations; unmoderated work can examine a stable pattern more broadly; follow-up interviews can diagnose selected recordings. Sequence is more important than declaring one mode superior.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: benefits application?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: An unmoderated study finds abandonment on an eligibility question. Possible causes include distrust, unclear language, ineligibility, missing documents, interruption, or fear of consequences. Moderated work can diagnose these explanations and protect participants.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Once wording and routes stabilise, unmoderated comparison may estimate directional differences, but it still cannot represent people who lack device access or never reach recruitment.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at operational quality?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Pilot both modes. For moderated sessions, calibrate moderators, scripts, assistance, consent, recording, note-taking, and safeguarding. For unmoderated work, test task comprehension without coaching, prototype resilience, device requirements, privacy, incentives, fraud checks, exclusion rules, and handling of partial data.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Report mode effects. Home context may be more natural but uncontrolled; lab attention may be artificial; think-aloud can slow action; asynchronous tasks may be interrupted. These are properties of evidence, not nuisances to hide.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at where this can go wrong?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Speed default: unmoderated scale replaces diagnosis and care. Moderator dependence: participants succeed because of subtle coaching. Task ambiguity: independent participants solve different imagined problems. False scale: sample size is mistaken for representativeness or causal explanation. Unsafe independence: sensitive or consequential tasks lack support and debriefing.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Hybrid duplication: two modes ask the same question without complementary value.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Design each mode for its actual evidence
turns.text: What changes when we look at design each mode for its actual evidence?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Unmoderated studies need a self-contained scenario, stable prototype, realistic content, reliable instrumentation, accessible task delivery, and a recovery plan for technical problems. They support broader conditions and natural timing but cannot explain every hesitation or safely manage serious misunderstanding. Open text is not a replacement for observation.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Analysis acknowledges mode effects. A moderator may increase persistence; remote unmoderated participants may abandon because of study technology; lab conditions may remove interruption. The decision report states what the method can and cannot support and chooses the next evidence accordingly.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: destructive account action?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: An unmoderated test can measure whether people find deletion, but moderated work is better for understanding consequence and emotional response. Neither should expose participants to actual irreversible loss merely to increase realism.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where does the harder design decision appear?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Senior practitioners budget for evidence quality, not session count. They ask who each mode systematically excludes: unmoderated platforms may exclude assistive technology, older devices, low bandwidth, limited literacy, or people uncomfortable recording. Moderated scheduling can exclude shift workers or carers.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Mitigate through alternative participation routes rather than describing exclusion as participant failure.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Match observation depth to the risk
turns.text: What changes when we look at match observation depth to the risk?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The team combines methods deliberately: moderated work discovers why “request received” is misread; unmoderated testing estimates how often a revised explanation supports correct choice. Safety, privacy, accessibility, recruitment, technical failure, and analysis limits are planned for both.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: <! -- Editorial: manual revision; curated product example --

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can we see that in a concrete product situation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Illustrative scenario: a complex loan comparison. An unmoderated test can scale a straightforward task, but it may not reveal why people misunderstand rate assumptions or feel pressured. Moderation lets the researcher probe reasoning without coaching. The choice depends on the learning risk, participant access, task complexity, and what the team can responsibly infer.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should I notice the next time I use a product?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Watch an unmoderated research clip or product recording. List three plausible explanations for the same visible hesitation. Which one could a moderator probe, and which requires evidence outside a session?
